forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Cheltenham council to fall £563,000 short of minimum reserves by March
news_drafts.lead: Cheltenham's general reserves are forecast to fall to £937,000 by 31 March 2027, leaving the council £563,000 below the level its Section 151 Officer, the chief finance officer, assesses as prudent. An £838,000 forecast overspend is the cause. At the same time, the council's capital programme — money spent on long-lived assets such as buildings — is being cut by 13.5%, from £42.96m to £37.1m. The National Cyber Innovation Centre at Golden Valley, budgeted at £32.85m, is unaffected and now represents 89 per cent of the entire capital spending plan. Separately, the Housing Revenue Account, which manages council housing and is funded by rents, is forecast to overspend by £650,000, driven by £465,000 in lost rental income from vacant properties and £201,000 in additional borrowing costs from higher interest rates.

findings.headline: Gloucestershire business rates pooling arrangement not financially beneficial following baseline reset
findings.detail: The council has determined that participation in a business rates pool with other Gloucestershire authorities offers no material financial benefit following the government's reset of business rates baselines and the limited growth available. The position will be reviewed annually by the Section 151 Officer under existing delegation.
findings.matters: Business rates pooling can be a material income source where growth is available; the reset has eliminated this benefit, removing a potential income offset to budget pressures.
findings.figures: None; decision based on baseline reset and limited growth outlook
findings.quote: Following the reset of business rates baselines and the limited level of business rates growth currently available within the system, participation in a Gloucestershire Business Rates Pool is not currently considered to provide a material financial benefit to the Council

findings.headline: Rising borrowing and treasury management costs identified as a principal ongoing pressure on base budget
findings.detail: Higher borrowing and treasury costs are identified as one of the principal pressures facing the council, with costs expected to continue rising. The report notes this will require careful management of the capital programme affordability, including major projects such as the National Cyber Innovation Centre and Golden Valley Development.
findings.matters: Structural and recurring cost pressure that will constrain available resources for service delivery and affects the sustainability of the budget over the medium term.
findings.figures: No specific quantum provided; assessed as principal pressure requiring treasury management attention
findings.quote: higher borrowing costs are expected to continue to place pressure on the Council's base budget

findings.headline: 2026/27 £838,000 overspend partly offset by approximately £750,000 of non-recurring staffing and service underspends
findings.detail: The council's reported overspend is mitigated by staffing vacancies (£500,000) and Housing and Communities service underspends (£250,000), which are explicitly noted as non-recurring. This indicates the underlying structural deficit is materially worse than the headline figure and will resurface when these gaps normalise.
findings.matters: The true structural deficit is masked by temporary staffing vacancies; when vacancies are filled and services return to normal activity, the council faces a significantly larger recurrent problem.
findings.figures: £838,000 overspend; £500,000 staffing underspends; £250,000 Housing and Communities underspends (both non-recurring)
findings.quote: The 2026/27 position benefits from a number of favourable variances which are largely non-recurring, including approximately £500,000 of staffing underspends and £250,000 within Housing and Communities

findings.headline: Only £222,565 of £1.054m 2026/27 savings target delivered; £456,185 (43%) still unidentified
findings.detail: Against a three-year savings target of £1.054m for 2026/27, the council has delivered only £222,565 to the August monitoring point, with a further £375,000 rated as at risk. The report identifies the delivery of further recurring savings as critical to both improving the current year and establishing a sustainable base for 2027/28.
findings.matters: Significant shortfall in executing planned savings indicates either unrealistic planning or delivery challenges; the council must find additional savings while already falling short on this year's targets.
findings.quote: £222,565 of savings had been delivered and assessed as green, with a further £375,000 assessed as amber and £456,185 still to be identified

findings.headline: General Balances forecast to fall to £937,000, £563,000 below the prudent minimum of £1.500m
findings.detail: The 2026/27 forecast General Fund overspend of £838,000 will require a transfer of £522,000 from General Balances, leaving a balance of £937,000. This falls below the minimum level the Section 151 Officer considers prudent to maintain financial resilience. The report states the council cannot sustainably rely on reserves to manage recurring budget pressures.
findings.matters: Reserves below the prudent minimum limit the council's capacity to absorb unexpected costs or emergencies, a key indicator of financial stability for lenders and peer authorities.
findings.quote: This is £563,000 below the £1.500m minimum level considered prudent by the Section 151 Officer
